planting.note: Direct sow fresh nuts in fall 2-3 inches deep in deep, well-drained loam in full sun; seed requires several months of cold stratification over winter and the seedling forms a deep taproot almost immediately, so transplanting older stock is difficult.

directions: Native to the mountains of Zhejiang and Anhui provinces in eastern China, this is the hickory grown commercially around the city of Lin'an for its thin-shelled, sweet-kerneled nuts, which are a popular roasted snack throughout China. Trees are slower to establish than pecan but tolerate a similar range of warm-summer, cold-winter climates, and grafted selections begin bearing years before seedling trees. Give it deep, fertile, well-drained soil and full sun, and expect a long juvenile period of a decade or more before significant nut production begins. Collectors of edible nut trees in the United States have begun trialing grafted Chinese hickory as a smaller-statured alternative to pecan with a markedly different, richer-flavored nut.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh nuts in fall into deep, well-drained, limestone-derived soil in full sun; seedlings develop a deep taproot quickly, so site trees in their permanent location rather than transplanting.

directions: Palmer hickory is a little-grown species native to limestone mountain slopes and oak-pine woodlands of northeastern Mexico, particularly the Sierra Madre Oriental of Nuevo Leon and Tamaulipas. It is the southernmost true hickory in North America and the least cold-hardy, making it suitable mainly for warm-temperate to subtropical gardens where pecan and shagbark hickory are marginal. The thick-shelled nuts are small but edible, and the species is sought mainly by rare-nut-tree collectors and botanical gardens building complete Carya collections rather than for commercial nut production. Plant in deep, well-drained, alkaline to neutral soil in full sun and protect young trees from hard freezes until well established.

planting.note: Direct sow fresh nuts in fall 2-3 inches deep in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, or stratify cold and moist over winter for spring sowing; young trees grow quickly and begin bearing well before most other walnuts.

directions: Native to central and western China, Chinese walnut is closely related to the Japanese walnut and Manchurian walnut but is recognized as a distinct species, with downy new growth, long pinnate leaves, and clustered, deeply ridged, thick-shelled nuts carried in long chains like those of its Japanese cousin. It is grown mainly by collectors and botanic gardens for its handsome tropical-looking foliage and fast, precocious growth rather than for serious nut production, since the kernel is small relative to the thick shell. Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with ample moisture, and allow generous room for its wide-spreading crown. Like other walnuts it produces juglone and should be sited away from juglone-sensitive plants such as tomatoes and apples.

planting.note: Sow fresh nuts in spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun at a cool, high-elevation or mild subtropical site; this species comes from frost-free to only lightly frosted Andean cloud forest and does not tolerate hard freezes.

directions: Andean walnut is a large timber and nut tree native to mid-elevation cloud forests of the northern Andes in Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru, where it is known as nogal and prized for its dark, richly figured wood as much as for its nuts. It needs a cool but essentially frost-free climate, making it suitable for mild subtropical or highland-tropical gardens rather than temperate ones where other walnuts thrive. The nuts are smaller than English walnut with a thick shell and are harvested locally, and the husks have traditionally been used to produce a dark dye called nogalina. Give it deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun and the generous room needed for a long-lived shade and specimen tree.
sources: Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations

planting.note: Sow fresh nuts in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; this subtropical montane species tolerates light frost once established but is damaged by hard freezes, so protect young trees in marginal zones.

directions: Argentine walnut is native to the Yungas cloud forests of the eastern Andean foothills of northwestern Argentina and adjacent Bolivia, where it grows alongside subtropical montane hardwoods at elevations with mild winters and humid summers. Long valued locally for its dark, fine-grained timber and for its small, thick-shelled but flavorful nuts, it is grown outside its native range mainly by collectors in mild-winter, frost-light climates such as coastal California or the Gulf Coast. Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, and give it room to develop its broad, spreading crown. As with all walnuts, its roots and fallen leaves release juglone, so keep sensitive garden plants at a distance.
sources: Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations

planting.note: Sow fresh nuts in spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun at an essentially frost-free site; this species comes from warm montane forest of southern Mexico and northern Central America and is damaged by freezing temperatures.

directions: Named for the Olancho region of Honduras, this walnut is native to mountain forests of southern Mexico, Guatemala, and Honduras, overlapping the northern edge of the Central American tropics. It is a large, long-lived timber tree with dark, decorative wood and small, thick-shelled, edible nuts gathered locally rather than traded commercially. Because it tolerates no more than the lightest frost, it is grown outside its native range only in frost-free or near-frost-free gardens, typically by botanical collections assembling a full range of New World walnut species. Plant in deep, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing the broad canopy plenty of room to develop over the tree's long lifespan.
sources: Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations
